blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: A single casual video leaves a moving scene under-determined: a point seen once from each place can slide toward or away from the camera and still match every frame. We constrain the reconstruction with the structure of the motion itself. Building on DynMF, we model a scene's motion as a handful of SE(3) trajectories, each rigid, and let every point follow one of them alone, never a blend. DynMF2 computes this factorization directly from 3D point trajectories, with no rendering, by Expectation-Maximization (EM). Its M-step fits, in closed form, every rigid motion to the points assigned to it, and its E-step reassigns every point to the motion that explains it with the least error. The background is simply one more motion, the camera's, so no masks are needed. Three tools then revise the factorization: requery adds trajectories where the rendering shows parts the tracker missed, merge joins motions that move together, and split separates those that do not. Thus the number of motions follows the scene. Without masks, DynMF2 clearly outperforms the mask-based baselines in view synthesis on iPhone and NVIDIA and in 3D tracking on iPhone. It recovers what masks leave out, from thin parts and details to small movers far in the background. Its motions segment the moving parts of MOVi-F and iTACO scenes competitively, although DynMF2 is never trained to segment. What moves in a scene is not decided in advance: it emerges from the rigid motions themselves.
blocks.zh: 单一的随机视频会让移动场景落空:从每个地方看到一次的点可以滑向相机或从相机上走去,仍然与每个相框相匹配. 我们用运动本身的结构来限制重建。 在DynMF的基础上,我们把一个场景的动作模拟成一小撮SE(3)的轨迹,每个刚性地,让每个点单独跟随其中之一,从不搞混. DynMF2直接从3D点轨迹计算出这种因子化,没有渲染,由Expectation-Maximization(EM). 它的M步以闭合的形式适合每一个刚性地运动到分配给它的分数,而它的E步将每一个分数重新分配给以最小错误解释它的运动. 背景只是又一个动作,相机的,所以不需要口罩. 3个工具随后修改了因子化:Requery在渲染显示跟踪器所错失的部分时会添加出轨迹,合并了一起移动的动作,并分拆了不移动的动作. 因此,动议的数量跟随现场。 没有口罩,DynMF2在iPhone和NVIDIA上的视图合成以及iPhone上的3D跟踪中明显地超过了基于口罩的基线. 它能收回面具留下的东西 从薄薄的零件和细节 到小移动器,在背景很深。 它的运动会以竞争的方式将MOVi-F和ITACO场景的移动部位分割开来,尽管DynMF2从未受过分会训练. 场景的动向不是事先决定的:它是从僵硬的动议中产生的。

blocks.en:
Casual video leaves this reconstruction under-determined. A single camera sees each point from one place at each
instant, so a point that drifts along its line of sight, or fades where it should be hidden, still matches every
training frame, and the error shows only from a new viewpoint. The motion model has to supply the constraint that the
views do not. Many models impose almost none: feed-forward networks predict a point map per
frame [ 103 , 81 ] , and deformation fields give each Gaussian its own
motion [ 98 , 86 ] . Others let every Gaussian blend a few shared motions, as global
bases [ 35 , 80 ] , scaffold nodes [ 38 ] or local bases in a
cluster [ 108 ] . Shape of Motion [ 80 ] argues that 3D scene motion
decomposes into a few rigid ones, yet a blend of rigid motions is not rigid. Each Gaussian moves on its own again, and a wrong motion can still fit the training views.

Most methods must also be told what moves. Shape of Motion and MotionScale separate moving objects from the static
background with masks, drawn from user clicks [ 80 , 95 ] or by
SAM2 [ 108 , 66 ] , and MoSca thresholds the epipolar error of optical
flow [ 38 ] . Whatever moves outside the masks or below the threshold, such as a person walking far in the
background, is reconstructed as static. The motions then come from a common recipe: lifted tracks are grouped once by
k-means on their positions or velocities, and Procrustes alignment fits each group with a rigid
motion [ 80 , 108 ] . The grouping never asks whether a rigid motion explains it,
and the fitted motions never send a track back to a better group. Training only partly repairs this first pass. Parts the tracker missed, often thin or fast ones, never get a motion of their own and borrow a
neighbour’s. They refine the motions of a grouping, not the grouping.

blocks.en:
Kratimenos et al . [ 35 ] showed that the motion of a scene factorizes into a few shared trajectories,
but learned those trajectories and each point’s weights from scratch, through the renderer. With today’s 3D tracks, both can be
computed before training starts.
We argue that the motion of most scenes is a few rigid SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) motions, and that a model should hold every
point to exactly one of them, never a blend. The restriction is deliberate: a point that cannot blend motions cannot
hide a wrong one either. We keep the common start, k-means and Procrustes, and take it one step further, into an EM that alternates
between fitting each motion to its tracks in closed form and moving each track to the motion that predicts it best,
until neither changes. The motions thus choose the grouping, and no mask is needed, since the static background is found
as one more motion. Three tools then keep revising it. Where the rendering disagrees with the video, DynMF2 requeries tracks
and gives them motions. It merges motions that move as one, static or not, and splits those that do not, so the number
of motions follows the scene.
Motion segmentation and 3D tracking come out of the model as by-products.

blocks.en:
We test DynMF2 on two benchmarks of monocular dynamic view synthesis, iPhone [ 18 ] and
NVIDIA [ 99 ] . Without masks, it renders new views at 18.05 and 23.83 dB masked PSNR, against
16.72 and 23.37 dB for Shape of Motion [ 80 ] , and tracks points in 3D with an
end-point error of 0.058 m, against 0.082 m. On MOVi-F [ 19 ] , without segmentation labels, its
motions segment scenes at 0.775 ARI, against 0.579 for the supervised Segment Any Motion [ 27 ] .
It keeps small movers, such as people walking far behind the subject ( Fig. 4 ), that methods built on masks
or thresholds freeze into the background. Our contributions are: • DynMF2, a monocular 4D reconstruction method that holds each Gaussian to exactly one of a few rigid SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) motions, with no masks and no separate static set. • To our knowledge the first dynamic Gaussian-splatting method whose motions are computed by EM rigid-motion segmentation
of 3D tracks: tracks are grouped by the rigid
motions that predict them, not by k-means alone, and requery, merge and split revise the groups, so that their
number follows the scene. • Extensive experiments and ablations on view synthesis, 3D tracking and motion segmentation, showing that hard
rigid motions found without masks compete with or beat methods that blend motions and are told what moves.

blocks.en:
DynMF [ 35 ] blends a few shared trajectories with per-Gaussian weights learned through the
renderer. A sparsity loss pushes each Gaussian towards one trajectory. Most later methods keep this mixture, with SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) bases [ 80 , 84 , 107 ] , hierarchies [ 45 , 39 , 82 ] or nearby nodes [ 28 , 38 , 104 , 106 , 100 , 87 ] , even when new bases appear where the render
error is high [ 105 ] , so no point commits to one motion and rigidity is only encouraged.
Others add a motion prior as a loss: a Gaussian process fitted to well-observed
Gaussians [ 34 ] , a graph in which low-uncertainty Gaussians guide the
rest [ 20 ] , or one rigid transform per object that a 2D segmenter
labels rigid [ 37 ] .
SP-GS [ 76 ] does commit each Gaussian to one rigid superpoint, but superpoints are many spatial patches,
driven by a deformation network to speed up rendering. MotionScale [ 108 ] commits from positions and
can then only cut: k-means gives hard clusters with soft local bases inside, which training splits and culls.
Articulat3D [ 21 ] commits each Gaussian to one part after a soft stage and reassigns it by
gradient, but its parts are the joints of one articulated object.
Grouped 4DGS [ 30 ] shares one transform within each group of splats and, from multi-view video,
splits groups and adds splats where render errors cluster. To our
knowledge, none merges motions or queries new tracks during training. DynMF2 instead computes the one-hot
weights and the rigid motions by EM on the 3D tracks before training starts, and training revises them in both
directions, with no masks or separate static set. Concurrently, RayCo4D [ 57 ] and XM4D [ 22 ] also blend nodes,
the latter computing their motions before rendering. MoSE3 [ 9 ] , also concurrent, brings SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) into point tracking: trained on synthetic data, it predicts 3D tracks, soft rigidity groups and per-pixel rigid transforms,
but reconstructs no scene.

blocks.en:
The factorization behind these models is far older. Under an orthographic camera, the tracks of a rigid scene form a
low-rank matrix [ 72 ] , and bases over shape or trajectory extend this to non-rigid
objects [ 4 , 1 , 74 , 110 ] . With several rigid
motions, each one’s tracks span their own subspace [ 10 , 36 ] , so finding the motions
becomes grouping the tracks. Subspace clustering fits these subspaces
algebraically [ 75 ] or writes each track as a sparse combination of the
others [ 14 ] . Spectral clustering of long tracks follows the same
pattern [ 5 , 58 ] . These methods return a partition, and the motions must be fitted
afterwards. Layered models instead alternate between assigning points to motions and refitting
them [ 79 , 3 , 83 , 73 ] , adding or removing models through
energies [ 29 , 11 , 68 ] , which yields both together. Our EM belongs to this
line, as does multi-body SLAM, which clusters rigid bodies in 3D while estimating their
motion [ 25 , 26 ] , and so does the training-free graph of MotionBits [ 65 ] . Learned models now segment moving objects from optical
flow [ 94 , 91 , 43 ] , from long tracks [ 27 ] or with
SAM [ 92 ] , and some carry these classical ideas into their losses, as EM [ 53 ] or as
low-rank grouping of trajectories [ 32 ] . Other methods also build the scene from the rigid pieces they find: from
monocular tracks [ 69 ] , with EM over RGB-D frames and object detections [ 71 ] , as
primitives cut by masks [ 52 ] , or as parts learned inside a radiance field [ 96 ] .
DynMF2 needs no masks or detections, and it computes its SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) segmentation from tracks instead of learning it
through the renderer; that segmentation is the motion model of the rendered scene.

blocks.en:
K K is set high so that every rigid part receives a motion, and most scenes end with more motions than rigid parts. The
background is the clearest case: EM often splits its points across several motions. The given cameras decide which
motions belong to it. A motion joins the background if the cameras alone explain its points within the error of the
background’s own points. No other motion ever joins it. Two of the remaining motions should be merged when one rigid
motion explains the points of both. We fit that motion to the union of their points with Eq. 4 and measure
how much the error of each motion’s points rises over that motion’s own fit. The scale of this rise comes from the
background itself. We cut two nearby patches from its points, with as many points as the two motions under test, and
fit them together. They share one motion, so their rise is only noise. A motion objects to a merge if its rise exceeds
that of every such pair and the background’s own error. The pair with the smallest rise merges first, and we repeat
until no pair passes. When two groups are tested, any motion they contain can object, not only the last one added.
Small differences therefore cannot add up along a chain.

blocks.en:
EM can also give one motion to two parts that move differently. This happens when they were close at initialisation,
or when one of them is too small to win a motion of its own. A motion is split when two rigid motions explain its points
better than one, by more than noise alone would allow. We run Eqs. 4 and 5 with two motions on its points,
several times from different first guesses, such as its worst-fitting points against the rest. Each run gives a cut. Its gain is the drop in the
error of the new side once that side receives its own motion. Noise sets the scale again, this time from the motion
itself. We build copies of its points that hold a single motion by construction: each point sits at the single motion’s
prediction plus its own residual under the cut, with a random sign. The same procedure runs on every copy. A cut passes
only if its gain exceeds that of every copy with a new side of similar size, and the passing cut with the largest gain
is made. The new motions are tested in turn, so K K grows without a cap.

blocks.en:
We train with the losses of Shape of Motion [ 80 ] : a photometric loss, a loss that keeps each Gaussian on its point’s 2D track, a depth loss and
a prior that keeps the motions smooth in time. Density control clones, splits and prunes Gaussians, and a new Gaussian
copies its parent’s motion. The number of motions and the assignment of every point therefore change only
through requery, merge and split.

blocks.en:
The tools run in a fixed order. Split and merge first revise the factorization that EM returns, before any rendering
exists. A short first stage then gives the rendering that requery needs. Merge runs once more, and every motion is refit

this factorization, starting again from one Gaussian per point.

已存在。 然后是短暂的第一阶段, 使渲染出重温的需要。 合并再运行一次,每个动议都会重现
以坚固的分数依次为4和6。 最终阶段,然后从
这个因子化,从每分一个高斯开始。

Table 1 compares DynMF2 with four methods. SoM, MoSca and MBGS blend several motions in every Gaussian, and

blocks.en:
A rendering can look right with the wrong motions, so we also score the motions themselves ( Tab. 2 ).
MOVi-F [ 19 ] renders rigid objects moving in a scene, and iTACO [ 62 ] shows articulated
objects, such as a microwave whose door turns about its hinge. DynMF2 runs on both exactly as for reconstruction, with the
same pipeline and settings and the datasets’ cameras, and we score the factorization that its final reconstruction starts from.

translation error (ADD, in cm) against the true motion, per pixel and per object. On MOVi-F the object behind every track is known, so we also compare the track assignments with the
objects by the adjusted Rand index (ARI), which counts the background too, and the mean IoU. We compare with Segment Any Motion [ 27 ] ,

the concurrent MoSE3 [ 9 ] , which predicts rigid groups directly.

assignment. Rather, it marks a limitation of the framework and points to promising future work: SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) motions

border.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
DynMF2 computes the motion factorization of a dynamic scene instead of learning it through the renderer. EM on 3D
trajectories gives each point a single rigid motion, and requery, merge and split revise the set of motions and the points
they hold. The scene needs no masks, each Gaussian moves rigidly with one motion, and the same motions segment what moves.
DynMF2 leads every metric of view synthesis and tracking in Tab. 1 , and its motions, never trained to segment, are competitive
with methods trained to do so.
blocks.zh:
DynMF2计算动态场景的运动因子化,而不是通过渲染器学习. EM 在三维
轨迹给每个点一个单一的刚性运动,并重压,合并和分出修正一组运动和分数
他们坚守。 场景不需要口罩,每个高斯人只用一动一动就僵硬地走动,移动的动作部分相同.
DynMF2在 Tab. 1 中领导了每一个度量的视图合成和跟踪,其运动从未受过分块训练,具有竞争力
并训练出这样做的方法。

blocks.en:
Depth is now the limit. With sensor depth the same pipeline renders better, and with the exact 3D trajectories of MOVi-F,
EM recovers the rigid parts almost exactly (supplement). The tools measure their errors in pixels only to shield the
factorization from depth errors. The factorization can also give something back: a scene moves by a few SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) transformations, a structure that point tracks lack. MoSE3 [ 9 ] learns an SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) motion and a
track for every pixel. A tracker could instead learn only the few motions of a scene and the assignment of each point, with
this EM inside its training loop. Trajectories and motions would then sharpen each other: better trajectories give cleaner
motions, and cleaner motions show the tracker where it went wrong.
blocks.zh:
